source.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
source.authors: Seyedarmin Azizi; Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo; Arya Fayyazi; Saeid Shokoufa; M. Pedram

page_placements.theme: Harm recognition can survive refusal failure

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses prior work on safety concentrated in response-token positions, but explicitly distinguishes that axis from its own experiments on recurrent computation loops. Its results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports extensive results on harmful compliance and refusal as inference loop count changes, plus related analyses and training interventions. These bear on a distinct recurrent-computation-depth finding, not the specified fine-tuning-on-harmful-or-benign-data, per-token KL, compliant-prefill/suffix/decoding, parameter/rank-localization, or response-token-depth claims. Prior results in Related Work are cited only and are not extracted as this paper's findings.
record.test_reason: The paper varies the number of recurrent inference loops in weight-tied models (Ouro, Huginn-0125). It does not fine-tune on harmful or benign data to erode safety, measure per-token KL, prefill responses, or localise safety in weights or ranks. It cites Qi et al. (2025) only to say that work is about token position, while its own axis is compute per token. The refusal-direction ablation acts on activations, not a small weight or rank set. The random-loop LoRA training spreads safety across loop depths, not response positions. None of its results measure what V1–V7 name.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. It should add three points. The effect is replicated on Huginn-0125 (1–32 loops). Dense-model layer removal loses task ability before refusal, the opposite order. Run-time repairs (the models' early-exit gate, per-request depth routing) do not help, while random-loop training removes the gap without hurting full-depth accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: No harmful-example fine-tuning safety-erasure recipe or response-token KL analysis is replicated. The paper changes inference-time recurrent loop count, probes and intervenes on activation states, and separately trains LoRA adapters with safety loss at selected loop depths.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with loop count, model checkpoint and training type; the text-quality filter affects shallow-cell sample sizes; prompt-template attacks combine with reduced depth. The paper also reports checks across generation protocols, a larger judge, and sampled decoding.

fits_no_version.finding: Reducing inference loops in recurrent-depth models raises harmful compliance and shrinks the refusal gap faster than task ability or harm detection fall. Dense layer removal shows the opposite order. The paper reports the same pattern on Huginn-0125 after final-loop safety training: compliance 0.031 at 32 loops vs 0.194 at 4 loops.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety trained at one recurrent depth does not carry to shallower inference depths in weight-tied models.

fits_no_version.finding: Harm is linearly readable after one loop (AUC ≥0.96), but the refusal direction has not settled. Ablating the direction at full depth removes refusal on Ouro-1.4B (0.950→0.130).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shallow-loop failure reflects an unsettled refusal direction, not missing harm information.

fits_no_version.finding: Jailbreak templates and reduced loops compose. Persona template plus one loop gives 0.830 compliance on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reduced recurrent depth amplifies prompt-level jailbreaks.

record.problems: The paper reports limited released recurrent-depth model sizes (1.4B to 3.5B parameters). Some shallow settings have small post-filter samples; the authors note one-loop filtering and judge reliability concerns. The generation-free forced-choice measurement shows no effect for Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, so its evidence there relies on filtered generation results. The safety-training mitigation was not repeated across multiple training seeds in the main experiments, although seed checks are reported for the Ouro-1.4B comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. The cited findings from prior work are not extracted as this paper's results. Additional recurrent-depth sweeps, routing experiments, training comparisons, and appendix checks were not included as rows because the selected rows capture the distinct findings relevant to the claim's subject without treating them as tests of its listed versions.

untested.parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning of an aligned model.
No benign fine-tuning measured for safety erosion. The LoRA training adds refusal data.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No response prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding attacks. Only prompt-template jailbreaks are tested, including an instructed 'Sure, here is' opening.
No weight or rank localisation. The single refusal direction is in activation space.
Does not examine whether data or objective cause token-position shallowness. It argues final-loop supervision causes depth-axis fragility, which is a different axis.
No token-position deepening. Random-loop training deepens across loop count, not response positions.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses call is correct. Qi et al. 2025 and other shallow-alignment work appear only in Related Work, and the paper distinguishes its compute axis from token position. Huginn and training-objective results (Tables 2, 6, 15, 16) are not rowed, but they bear on no version, so they are not listed under missing. The forced-choice 'Sure, here is' versus refusal comparison is a depth-sweep measure, not a prefill attack.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples is tested for erosion of pre-existing safety.
No ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction-data fine-tuning is tested for increased harmful compliance.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is measured.

No compliant-token prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding change is tested as a way past initial response tokens. Prompt-template attacks are tested, but do not measure this version's named mechanisms.
The paper intervenes on a refusal direction in activation state, not a small set of weights or ranks.
Training at different recurrent loop depths is studied, but not whether training data or objectives cause safety to be shallow across response-token positions.
Random-loop safety training is tested across recurrent computation depths, not training that spreads safety across response-token positions.

rows.subject: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking
rows.stage_stated: Thinking; extra reasoning training; trained with 4 loops
rows.operation_detail: Add the refusal direction u with coefficient 0.2 to the state at one loop.
rows.note: Harmful compliance changes from 0.680 to 0.090; harmless refusal changes from 0.490 to 0.690; refusal gap changes from -0.170 to +0.220. Random direction control leaves the gap at -0.050.
rows.check: This is activation steering with a refusal direction. The paper notes it is selective only on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking: on the other two checkpoints the gap barely moves (-0.100→-0.050 and +0.350→+0.370). No row records those two results.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog versions; adding the activation direction at one loop with coefficient 0.2 raises harmful-prompt refusal from 0.320 to 0.910.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, including its continuation after Figure 9.
source_check.problem: Activation steering does not establish safety training beyond early response tokens; no claim version is linked.

rows.subject: Ouro-2.6B-Thinking

rows.baseline: 0.080 at 4 loops with no template; 0.717 at 4 loops with persona template; 0.447 at 1 loop with no template
rows.note: The study tests a prompt template, not a compliant-token prefill or suffix.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog versions; persona-template compliance at one loop=0.830, versus 0.717 with persona at four loops and 0.080 without a template at four loops.
source_check.problem: Persona prompting combined with fewer recurrent loops does not establish the opening-bypass mechanism of V4; no version is linked.

rows.subject: Ouro-2.6B-Thinking
rows.stage_stated: Thinking; extra reasoning training; trained with 4 loops
rows.operation_detail: Apply the prompt template instructing the model to begin with “Sure, here is”, with one loop.
rows.note: This is an instruction to start with a phrase, not a prefilled compliant response token sequence.
rows.check: This is a prompt instruction to begin with 'Sure, here is', not a prefilled compliant opening, so it is not V4's mechanism. The full-depth prefix-injection effect (0.080→0.298 on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, Table 10) is a jailbreak-template result, not a prefill test. Its versions stay none.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog versions; compliance at one loop=0.671 with the prefix instruction versus 0.447 without it.
source_check.problem: An instruction requesting a compliant opening does not demonstrate bypass by an actual prefilled opening; no version is linked.

relation.reason: Section 8 discusses shallow safety alignment and explicitly distinguishes its response-position axis from this study's recurrent-loop axis, with token positions and decoding settings held fixed.

tranche.reason: The study tests recurrent computation depth and activation interventions. Its training comparison supervises different loop readouts rather than response-token positions. These results do not test the listed claim versions.

source_check.notes: All listed numerical results and both synthesis statements match the text. State corrections concern applicability to the catalog claim versions, not whether the reported recurrent-depth or activation effects occurred.
